title: How the US Navy Is Actually Going to Blockade the Entire Strait of Hormuz
fullText: The United States Navy just did something it has not done on this scale since the Cold War. It put a choke hold on an entire country using warships. Not an air strike, not a bombing run. A full maritime blockade. As of 10:00 in the morning Eastern time on Monday, no ship enters or leaves Iranian ports. No tanker carrying Iranian oil reaches its buyer. No vessel that paid Iran's cryptocurrency toll is safe on open international waters. Two aircraft carrier strike groups, the USS Gerald R. Ford, the USS Abraham Lincoln. Each one is surrounded by its own pack of destroyers, cruisers, submarines, and support vessels. Roughly 60 warships in total, more firepower concentrated in a single stretch of ocean than most countries have in their entire military. All of it aimed at one narrow waterway on the southern edge of Iran. And the question almost nobody is asking is the one that actually matters. How does this actually work? What happens Monday morning? What does a real naval blockade in 2026 against a country with drones and cryptocurrency toll booths and a supply line to China actually look like in practice? By the end of this video, you will fully understand exactly how the United States Navy is going to shut down the most important shipping lane on Earth. Ship by ship, tanker by tanker. What ships are doing the work? What happens when a vessel refuses to stop? Why 40 American allies just refuse to help? And why this operation could end the Iranian regime or blow up into a full regional war within the next 10 days. Let us start with what a naval blockade actually is. Because most people have heard the word but have never seen what it looks like in practice. A blockade is not bombing. It is not an invasion. It is the use of warships to physically prevent other ships from entering or leaving a specific area of ocean. Imagine a police cordon, but at sea. The Navy positions its vessels across the entrances to a country's ports. Every ship that tries to come in or go out has to pass through that cordon. Warships radio the captain. They order the ship to slow down, identify itself, and state its cargo and destination. If the cargo is banned, if the destination is banned, or if the ship refuses to cooperate, armed sailors board the vessel. They take control of the bridge, they inspect every part of the ship. If the cargo confirms what the Navy suspected, the ship is turned around or seized. That is what a blockade is. It is police work at sea, except the police have missiles, and the suspects can be oil tankers the size of small cities. Now, here is where it gets really interesting. The United States did not declare a blockade of Iran alone. Trump was very specific in his announcement. The blockade covers two categories of ships. Category 1 is any vessel trying to enter or leave an Iranian port. Those ships get stopped. No exceptions. Category 2 is something much bigger and far more aggressive. Any vessel anywhere on the high seas that has paid a toll to Iran for passage through the Straight of Hormuz is now a target for interdiction. That second category changes the geographic scope of the operation by an order of magnitude. A Chinese flagged tanker carrying Iranian oil to a refinery in Shanghai, already 2,000 mi from the strait, can now be intercepted by the United States Navy because it paid a fee to the Revolutionary Guard before leaving the Gulf. The blockade is not just in Hormuz. The blockade is wherever the United States Navy can reach the ship. This is where the Ford and the Lincoln become the center of everything. An aircraft carrier is not a ship. It is a floating city. Over a thousand ft long, roughly 5,000 sailors living and working on board. 70 to 90 combat aircraft in the hangar deck below. Think of it as a mobile military base parked in international waters off the coast of a country it is now strangling. Each carrier brings its own strike group, a collection of other warships that exist mainly to protect it and extend its reach. Each group includes three guided missile destroyers, at least one guided missile cruiser, a nuclearpowered attack submarine running silent somewhere nearby, and supply vessels keeping the whole force fed and fueled. Among those destroyers, two are worth understanding in detail. The USS Frank E. Peterson and the USS Michael Murphy. Both are Arley Burke class destroyers and both have already entered the Strait of Hormuz. On April 11th, they completed the first American warship transit through the straight since the war began. Each one displaces over 9,000 tons, stretches more than 500 ft, and can move at over 30 knots, which is roughly the speed of a very fast cargo ship. Each one carries 96 missiles ready to launch in seconds. A mix of anti-aircraft, anti-ship, land attack, and anti-ubmarine weapons, plus a 5-in gun, a radar guided rotary cannon that can shoot down incoming drones at the last second, and torpedoes. What ties all of this together is something called Eegis. Eegis is a combat system that lets one ship see through the radars of every other ship and aircraft in the formation. If one radar picks up a drone coming in, every destroyer in the strike group sees it at the same instant. The whole formation fights as oneworked weapon. But here is the problem. None of this hardware matters if the ships stopping tankers cannot actually get through the straight without hitting a mine. And that is why the blockade is not just a surface operation. Underneath the warships, beneath the waterline, there is a second operation running continuously, mine clearance. Remember, Iran laid hundreds of naval mines in the straight of Hormuz during the early weeks of the war. American intelligence believes Iran does not have a complete record of where those mines were placed because the operation was rushed and because tidal currents have shifted mines from their original positions. Every surface warship that moves through the straight is moving through water that has not been declared safe. That means the blockade has to carry its mine clearance force with it. The tools are aircraft, helicopters, and drones working together. P8 Poseidon aircraft, which are converted Boeing passenger jets, fly low grids dropping sensor boys that map the seafloor with sound. The MH53 Sea Dragon is a heavy helicopter that drags mind triggering equipment through the water, tricking mines into exploding harmlessly behind it. Underwater drones work the seafloor for days without human operators. Every new surveyed area expands the safe corridor the destroyers can move through. It is slow work, but it is the physical foundation of everything happening above the water line. Now, here is what happens when the blockade actually makes contact with a target ship. Picture an oil tanker carrying Iranian crude flagged in Panama, crewed by a mix of Indian and Filipino sailors heading east toward Asia. Somewhere in international waters, an American destroyer intercepts the tanker on its radar hundreds of miles out. The destroyer closes the distance, meaning it moves toward the tanker at combat speed. At roughly 20 m out, the destroyer sends a radio call. It identifies itself, states that the tanker is believed to have paid an illegal toll to Iran, and orders the vessel to stop engines and prepare for boarding. The tanker captain has a choice. comply, which means stopping engines, lowering a ladder, and allowing a boarding team to come aboard, or refuse. If the captain complies, a small inflatable boat drops off the destroyer side carrying 10 to 15 heavily armed sailors. They motor across, climb the ladder, and take control of the bridge. They check paperwork, inspect cargo, and question the crew. If evidence confirms an illegal toll payment, the tanker is rerouted or seized. If the captain refuses to stop, the destroyer escalates, warning shots across the bow, disabling the engines with guided weapons, or boarding under fire if authorized. Refusal carries real consequences. Iran's response to all of this has been loud, defiant, and almost completely detached from its actual military capacity. Within hours of Trump's announcement, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy issued a statement through Iranian state media. Any military vessel approaching the Strait of Hormuz will be considered a violation of the ceasefire and will be dealt with quote harshly and decisively. The Strait, the statement continued, is under the smart management of Iran's Navy. Now, stop and think about what that sentence means. Iran's Navy. The Navy that lost over 120 warships in 39 days of American and Israeli operations. The Navy whose Supreme Commander was killed. The Navy whose mind layer fleet is sitting on the seafloor where it was sunk in March. That Navy is telling the United States Navy what it will and will not permit in a waterway that the United States just deployed two carrier strike groups to control. There is another angle that almost nobody is talking about. Iran's threats right now are not empty in the sense that they cannot do anything. They are empty in the sense that anything they do will almost certainly accelerate their own collapse. If Iran fires on an American destroyer, the United States response would not be proportional. It would be overwhelming. Trump's truth social post included the exact phrase, "Anyone who fires at us or at a peaceful vessel will be blown to hell." That is not diplomatic language. That is a public commitment. Iran knows this. The Revolutionary Guard knows this. Their threats are designed for domestic Iranian audiences and for China and Russia, not for American planners. The threats are rhetoric. The blockade is reality. That gap between what Iran says and what Iran can actually do is the central fact of this entire situation. Think about what that means from Iran's perspective right now. Their navy is gone. Their air force is gone. Their Supreme Leader is dead. Their mine layers are on the bottom of the sea. Their mine records are incomplete. Their allies are now being threatened by the United States for shipping weapons that were supposed to help them. And the country that is supposed to be rescuing them economically, China, just saw its largest foreign oil supplier cut off by the same blockade that is strangling Thrron. Is this situation going to end in a controlled Iranian surrender within the next 10 days? or is Iran going to try one more military escalation even though it has almost nothing left to escalate with? Write your answer in the comments because the people who say Iran is about to fold and the people who say Iran always fires one last shot are going to have a serious argument under this video. And it gets worse for Iran because the economic target of the blockade is not really the Iranian military anymore. It is Carg Island. Carg is a small piece of land in the Persian Gulf that handles roughly 90% of all Iranian oil exports. Every major Iranian crude shipment passes through the pipelines, storage tanks, and loading terminals on carg. Without carg, Iran cannot sell oil. Without oil sales, Iran cannot pay its soldiers, cannot fund its proxies, cannot purchase food imports, cannot keep its economy running. The blockade does not need to destroy Carg to it. The blockade just needs to prevent any tanker from leaving Carg with crude on board. A storage facility full of oil that cannot leave port is just a very expensive, very slow motion way for a regime to run out of money. Analysts estimate that Iran's hard currency reserves, the dollars and euros it needs to import essential goods, can last roughly 60 to 90 days under a full blockade. After that, the regime faces a choice between internal collapse and a dramatic escalation it cannot afford. But here is what nobody in the American media is telling you clearly. The United States is doing this largely alone. The United Kingdom publicly refused to join the blockade within hours of Trump's announcement. France went further. President Mron called the blockade militarily unrealistic and said that any vessel trying to move through a forcibly open straight would be exposed to Iranian coastal fire. A coalition of over 40 nations, mostly the United States closest allies, had already formed a separate initiative 2 weeks before the blockade was announced. That coalition, led by the United Kingdom, includes France, Germany, Italy, Canada, Japan, and the United Arab Emirates. Its plan for reopening the strait does not involve a blockade. It involves diplomatic pressure, United Nations action, and economic sanctions if Iran does not reopen the waterway voluntarily. 40 of America's closest friends looked at Trump's plan and said, "We are not coming with you." This is where the conversation fundamentally changes. For decades, American military operations in the Middle East have been coalition operations. Desert Storm had 35 countries. Iraq in 2003 had 46. The fight against ISIS had over 70. The Hormuz blockade, the most ambitious American naval operation in the region in a generation, is being run by the United States with support from Israel and a handful of Gulf partners. That is it. The transatlantic alliance that has underpinned every major American military effort since the Second World War is openly refusing to participate. 40 American allies have chosen a different path. Is America going this alone going to work? Or does the refusal of 40 allies to join mean the blockade collapses before it finishes the job? One camp says the United States Navy has more firepower in the region than all 40 of those allies combined and that the mission does not need their help. The other camp says that allies refusing means legitimacy problems, diplomatic costs, and that blockades historically fall apart when enforcing nations run out of patience. write where you stand in the comments because that argument is coming. And there is one more factor that almost nobody is connecting yet. China, the single biggest buyer of Iranian oil. Before the war, Iran shipped roughly 1.4 million barrels of crude per day to China. During the war, that dropped but did not stop. Chinese tankers kept moving through the straight, paying Iran's toll, carrying Iranian oil to refineries on the Chinese coast. Those shipments supplied about 13% of China's total oil imports. Under the blockade, every single one of those tankers becomes a target. The United States Navy will now interdict Chinese flagged vessels in international waters based on whether they paid an Iranian toll. China has already responded not with military threats but with economic moves. Beijing cut refinery runs at Cineipek by 10%. It banned fuel exports. It implemented its largest domestic fuel price increase since 2022. China is preparing for a sustained loss of Iranian oil, which means China has quietly concluded that the blockade is serious enough to be real. The situation as of today looks like this. Two carrier strike groups are on station. Destroyers are already transiting the straight. Mine clearing operations are continuing 24 hours a day. The blockade is in effect. Iran is threatening retaliation, but cannot realistically afford to follow through. 40 American allies have refused to join. China is quietly preparing for Iranian oil to disappear from its supply chain. Oil is above $13 per barrel. Gas in the United States is at $4.13 per gallon, up 38% since February. Goldman Sachs has called this, in a published report, the largest oil supply shock in recorded history. And Iran's internal clock, the clock measuring how long the regime can survive without oil revenue, is now running out at roughly $30 million per day in lost exports. The blockade is not a single event. It is a continuous operation designed to tighten over time. Week one establishes the cordon and intercepts the first tankers. Week two chokes the financial flow. Week three is when the Iranian economy begins to show visible stress. By the end of the first month, American planners expect the regime to face a binary choice. come back to the table on American terms and abandon the nuclear program or escalate militarily and invite strikes on Carg Island and the nuclear program itself that Trump has publicly hinted at. So here's the question that matters. two carrier strike groups, 60 warships, a navy that lost its fleet and its leader, 40 allies on the sidelines, an oil buyer in China quietly cutting its losses, a regime that has roughly 90 days of reserves before the money runs out, and a president who has said publicly that his military is fully locked and loaded and ready to finish the little that is left of Iran. How does this end? Does the Iranian regime collapse under the economic pressure of the blockade within the next 60 to 90 days, forced back to the table with nothing left to bargain with? Or does Iran attempt one last military escalation, firing on an American warship or striking a Gulf oil facility, triggering the kind of American response that ends the regime through direct military force. One side says the blockade finishes this quietly. The other side says Iran never goes down without firing one final shot. Write your answer in the comments because the people who say economic collapse and the people who say one last war are about to have the most important argument on this channel. And if you have not seen our video on why the United States Navy cannot clear the mines in the Straight of Hormuz, and why the ships designed for that job were sent to a scrapyard 5 months before the war began, make sure to watch that one Next.

Nếu một radar phát hiện được một máy bay không người lái đang tiến tới, mọi tàu khu trục trong cuộc tấn công nhóm nhìn thấy nó cùng một lúc. Toàn bộ đội hình chiến đấu như một vũ khí thống nhất. Các công cụ là máy bay, trực thăng và máy bay không người lái làm việc cùng nhau.
